title: The man who memorised nonsense
text: Hermann Ebbinghaus learned nonsense syllables like WID and ZOF and tested his recall. Forgetting was steep at first, then slowed. Much was gone in a day or two.
em: gone in a day or two
source: Hermann Ebbinghaus, Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology (1885)
more:
He did this in the 1880s and used nonsense on purpose, so meaning and prior knowledge couldn't help. He was his only subject, a real limitation, but a 2015 replication by Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros found a very similar curve.

Meaningful material fades more slowly than nonsense, so his exact percentages aren't gospel. The shape holds: a steep loss early, then a long, slow tail. The next cards cover what slows it down.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

title: Spacing won 259 of 271
text: A 2006 review compared spaced study with cramming, same total time. Spacing won in 259 of 271 comparisons. Few findings in learning research are this reliable.
source: Cepeda et al., Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks, Psychological Bulletin (2006)
more:
Ebbinghaus noticed the spacing effect himself, and it has replicated for well over a century, across ages, subjects and even other species.

Why it works is still debated. One idea: letting a memory fade a little before you revisit it forces harder recall, which strengthens it more. The best gap depends on how long you need to remember. Later work by Cepeda and colleagues suggests very roughly 10 to 20 percent of that time, shrinking proportionally for longer horizons.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

title: Rereaders won for five minutes
text: Students either reread a passage or took practice tests on it. After five minutes, rereaders did slightly better. After a week, testers remembered far more.
source: Roediger & Karpicke, Test-Enhanced Learning, Psychological Science (2006)
more:
It's called the testing effect, or retrieval practice. Pulling something out of memory changes the memory and makes it easier to find next time.

It works best with spacing, and with feedback so mistakes don't stick. It even helps when you fail to recall, as long as you check the answer after. Closing the book and writing down what you remember counts. So does answering a flashcard out loud before flipping it.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

title: Learning painters by shuffling them
text: People learned painters' styles one artist at a time, or shuffled together. Shuffling did better at recognising new paintings. Most people still believed one-at-a-time had helped more.
author: Nate Kornell and Robert Bjork
source: Learning Concepts and Categories, Psychological Science (2008)
more:
Nate Kornell and Robert Bjork ran this in 2008. Shuffling is called interleaving, and it makes you notice what makes each thing different. Doug Rohrer and colleagues found the same in maths: students who practised mixed problem sets did much better on later tests, because they had to work out which method each problem needed.

Interleaving feels slower and messier, and early performance looks worse. That's a big part of why people avoid it.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

title: Why easy studying fools you
text: Robert Bjork's desirable difficulties: spacing, testing and mixing feel clumsy but make learning last. Rereading feels smooth, and we mistake that smoothness for mastery.
em: we mistake that smoothness for mastery
author: Robert A. Bjork
source: Memory and metamemory considerations in the training of human beings, in Metacognition (1994)
more:
We judge learning by how fluent it feels. Rereading makes a chapter familiar, and familiarity feels like knowing. But recognising something on the page is very different from producing it on a blank sheet.

Not every difficulty is desirable. Bjork's point is that a difficulty helps when it makes you do the mental work you'll need later, like recalling and telling things apart. Confusing explanations or background noise are just hard.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

text: …without looking at the book, try'd to compleat the papers again … Then I compared my Spectator with the original, discovered some of my faults, and corrected them.
author: Benjamin Franklin
source: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, part one (written 1771)
more:
As a teenager, Franklin taught himself to write by rebuilding essays from The Spectator. He jotted short hints, waited a few days, rewrote the essay without looking, then compared his version with the original and fixed his mistakes.

He varied it too. He turned some essays into verse and later back into prose to stretch his vocabulary. He also jumbled his notes, then tried to restore their order, to learn how to structure an argument.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

title: Make It Stick, boiled down
text: Make It Stick boils decades of learning research into a few habits. Quiz yourself instead of rereading. Space reviews out. Mix topics. Try answering before you're taught.
author: Peter C. Brown, Henry Roediger and Mark McDaniel
source: Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning (2014)
more:
Put together: after a lecture or chapter, close it and write what you remember. Check against the source and note the gaps, like Franklin. Review a few days later, then a week after that, mixing in older material.

The authors, Peter Brown, Henry Roediger and Mark McDaniel, also stress calibration: use tests to find out what you actually know. Most people who try it discover they knew less than they thought.

thread.title: How to learn so it sticks, in 7 cards

text: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
author: Francis Bacon
source: Essays, 'Of Studies' (1625 edition)
more:
In Bacon's English, conference means conversation and debate, and exact means precise. Reading stocks your mind. Talking with others makes you quick with what you know. Writing pins vague ideas down, because a sentence on paper can't hide behind a feeling of understanding.

Many people only find out they don't understand something when they try to explain it in writing and get stuck halfway.

text: As the art of reading … is the art of skipping, so the art of being wise is the art of knowing what to overlook.
author: William James
source: The Principles of Psychology, vol. 2, ch. 22 'Reasoning' (1890)
more:
James is describing how expert thinking works. As you get better at something, you stop processing every detail and see only the features that matter. A strong chess player glances at a board and ignores most of it. A beginner has to consider every piece.

Skimming to find what matters, then reading that part slowly, is a skill. The hard part is choosing what to overlook, and that depends on knowing what you're after.

text: …to divide each of the difficulties under examination into as many parts as possible, and as might be necessary for its adequate solution.
em: into as many parts as possible
author: René Descartes
source: Discourse on the Method, part II (1637; trans. John Veitch)
more:
Descartes set himself four rules for thinking. Accept nothing as true that you don't clearly know. Break each difficulty into parts. Work from the simplest parts up. Review everything so nothing is left out. This is the second.

'Write the report' is paralysing. 'List the five sections' isn't. The phrase 'as might be necessary' matters: the aim is to keep splitting until each piece is something you can actually do or answer.

text: People are generally better persuaded by the reasons which they have themselves discovered than by those which have come into the mind of others.
author: Blaise Pascal
source: Pensées, no. 10 (1670; trans. W. F. Trotter)
more:
Telling someone an answer, however clearly, hands them a conclusion with no roots. Helping them find it gives them a path back to it.

Learning research points the same way. The generation effect, studied since the 1970s, shows that information you produce yourself, even from small cues, is remembered better than information you just read. In the pensée before this one, Pascal adds a tip: to correct someone, first find the side from which they're right and admit it.

title: The man with a hammer
text: Charlie Munger said isolated facts are nearly useless without a latticework of big ideas from many fields. Know only one, and every problem looks like a nail.
em: every problem looks like a nail
author: Charlie Munger
source: A Lesson on Elementary Worldly Wisdom, talk at USC Business School (1994)
more:
His examples of models included compound interest, incentives, feedback loops and margin of safety. Problems don't arrive sorted into academic departments. A business problem can be part psychology and part maths.

Munger suggested learning the big ideas from each major field well enough to use them, then checking a problem against several. He reckoned around 80 or 90 important models do most of the work.

title: Invert, always invert
text: Instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, and avoid that. Charlie Munger took the habit from the mathematician Carl Jacobi.
author: Charlie Munger
source: Commencement speech at the Harvard School, Los Angeles (1986)
more:
In a 1986 graduation speech, Munger described a good life by listing sure routes to a miserable one, like envy, resentment and unreliability. Our minds spot what's clearly wrong faster than they design what's ideal. Ask how to make a team miserable and answers come fast: unclear priorities, surprise deadlines.

Jacobi used the idea in maths, where attacking a problem from its converse or negation often makes it easier. Proof by contradiction is the same move.

title: The cost of a quick check
text: Switch tasks and part of your mind stays on the last one. Sophie Leroy calls it attention residue. Even a quick inbox check leaves some.
author: Cal Newport
source: Deep Work, part 1 (2016)
more:
In Leroy's 2009 experiments, people who left one task unfinished and moved to another did worse on the second, because their thoughts kept drifting back.

Cal Newport builds on this in Deep Work. He argues that focusing without distraction on hard tasks is getting rarer just as it gets more valuable. His fixes are structural: schedule focus blocks in advance, batch shallow work like email, and treat focus as a skill that weakens without use.

title: A good bet can still lose
text: Former poker champion Annie Duke calls it resulting: judging a decision by how it turned out. A drunk driver who gets home safely still made a bad choice.
author: Annie Duke
source: Thinking in Bets, ch. 1 (2018)
more:
Her fix is to judge the decision separately from the outcome. What did you know at the time, and how did you weigh the odds? Learning only from outcomes means learning the wrong lessons from luck.

She opens her book with the pass at the end of the 2015 Super Bowl that was intercepted and instantly branded one of the worst calls ever. It would have been praised if it had worked, and a close look at the odds suggests it was defensible.

title: Growth mindset, smaller than advertised
text: Carol Dweck's research suggests people who see ability as something that grows handle setbacks better. Large recent studies say the effect on school results is real but modest.
author: Carol Dweck
source: Mindset: The New Psychology of Success (2006)
more:
Dweck contrasts a fixed mindset, where failure shows your limits, with a growth mindset, where failure tells you what to practise next. Praising effort and strategy instead of talent was one of her best-known recommendations.

The evidence got more nuanced. A 2018 meta-analysis found weak overall links between mindset and achievement. A large 2019 US national study found a short online mindset lesson raised grades slightly, mostly for lower-achieving students.

title: Everyone's thesis took longer
text: Psychology students guessed their senior theses would take about 34 days. Even their worst-case guesses averaged under 49. The real average was 55.5 days.
source: Buehler, Griffin & Ross, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1994)
more:
That was a 1994 study, and only about 30% finished within the time they'd predicted. Kahneman and Tversky named this the planning fallacy in 1979. We plan by picturing the steps going roughly as intended, and underweight the dull fact that they rarely do.

The best-known fix is reference class forecasting. Start from how long similar projects actually took, for you or others, then adjust a little for what's genuinely different.

title: Chesterton's fence
text: Chesterton's reformer finds a fence across a road, sees no use for it, and wants it gone. A wiser one says: first find out why it's there.
em: first find out why it's there
author: G. K. Chesterton
source: The Thing, 'The Drift from Domesticity' (1929)
more:
G. K. Chesterton wrote this in 1929. Rules and habits often exist because of a problem nobody remembers anymore, precisely because the fence solved it. Remove it and the problem can come back.

That doesn't mean every fence is wise. The burden is to understand before removing, and often the reason is long gone and the fence can go.

title: Can you really multitask?
text: Plenty of people say they're good at doing several things at once. What's actually happening in your head when you think you're multitasking?
source: Monsell, Task switching, Trends in Cognitive Sciences (2003)
more:
For anything that needs attention, you're mostly switching. Each switch costs something: in lab tasks, people are slower and make more errors right after changing tasks than after repeating one, even when warned a switch is coming.

Each cost is small, often a fraction of a second, but it adds up over a day of toggling and grows with harder tasks. The exception is pairing something automatic with something that needs thought, like walking while talking.

title: Are you a visual learner?
text: Most teachers and students believe people learn best in their preferred style: visual, auditory or hands-on. Does matching teaching to someone's style actually help?
em: learn best in their preferred style
source: Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer & Bjork, Psychological Science in the Public Interest (2008)
more:
There's no good evidence that it does. In 2008 a panel led by Harold Pashler set out what a proper test needs: sort learners by style, teach each group in more than one style, and check if each does best in its own. Very few studies did this, and those that did mostly found no such match.

People do have preferences, and some subjects suit some formats. Maps are visual. Music is auditory. The best format depends more on the content than the person.

title: Is 10,000 hours the magic number?
text: Malcolm Gladwell's Outliers made 10,000 hours of practice famous as the path to expertise. Is practice really what separates the best from everyone else?
source: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald, Psychological Science (2014)
more:
Partly. Practice matters a lot, but 10,000 isn't a rule. Anders Ericsson, whose violin research inspired the idea, said Gladwell oversimplified it: the figure was an average at one age, and the kind of practice mattered as much as the amount.

A 2014 meta-analysis by Brooke Macnamara and colleagues found deliberate practice explained about 26% of performance differences in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education and under 1% in professions.
